Dmitri Shostakovich. The Soviet Russian composer and pianist from 1906 to 1975, he was one of the most celebrated and scrutinized figures of twentieth-century music. Operating under the highly restrictive censorship of Joseph Stalin's regime, Shostakovich developed a unique musical language characterized by sharp contrasts, dark irony, grotesque humor, and hidden political subversion. His vast output includes fifteen symphonies, fifteen string quartets, and multiple operas, which alternate between public loyalty to the Soviet state and private grief and defiance.

Symphony No. 5 in D minor from 1937 is his most famous work, composed as a response to official condemnation. A journalist subtitled it as a Soviet artist's creative response to just criticism. Its apparently triumphant finale is often interpreted as forced, hollow jubilation. Symphony No. 7 in C major, the Leningrad symphony from 1941, was written during the German siege of the city and became a global symbol of resistance to fascism. It features a repetitive, mechanical invasion theme in the first movement that builds to a colossal climax. Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District from 1934 is a dark opera whose depiction of murder and raw sexuality outraged Stalin. This provoked the infamous 1936 Pravda editorial titled Muddle Instead of Music, which began Shostakovich's lifelong fear of arrest and execution.

String Quartet No. 8 in C minor from 1960 was written in Dresden after he reluctantly joined the Communist Party. It is dedicated to the victims of fascism and war. The work heavily incorporates his personal musical signature motif, DSCH: D, E-flat, C, and B natural. Symphony No. 13 in B-flat minor, the Babi Yar symphony from 1962, sets the poetry of Yevgeny Yevtushenko to commemorate the Nazi massacre of Jews at Babi Yar. It openly criticizes Soviet antisemitism and bureaucracy. Testimony is a highly controversial memoir published posthumously in 1979 by Solomon Volkov, which portrays the composer as a secret dissident who hid anti-Soviet double meanings in his music.

Shostakovich's orchestration and symphonic scale were heavily influenced by Gustav Mahler. He was the chief contemporary and rival of Sergei Prokofiev in the Soviet Union, and both navigated the dangerous shifting politics of the Soviet music authorities.
